title: Draupadi's swayamvara
hook: Karna strings the bow, and one sentence stops him

segments.voice: Yesterday, Draupadi's swayamvara: the stiff bow, the mark set high, and kings thrown to the floor — the kings fall, one by one. Did you ask who designed a test? Day seven hundred forty-two.

This week opened in the lac house. Since then: a tunnel dug in secret, a fire lit from inside, a family carried through the forest, a boat at the river, Bhima awake under a tree, a princess born from a fire, and a bow that throws kings to the floor. Now, as the kings give up, a man rises whom we've met before. Karna. Found in a basket on the river, raised by a charioteer, born with armor on his body. He walks to the bow.

In the version Ganguli translated, Karna lifts the bow and strings it. He fits the arrows. He's about to shoot. And Draupadi speaks, loudly, so the whole arena hears. In paraphrase: I will not choose a suta for my husband. A suta: a charioteer, a charioteer's son. Karna laughs, a bitter laugh, the text says. He glances up at the sun. And he puts the bow down. That's all. A few lines. And they land on everything we've heard about Karna these past weeks. The basket on the river. Adhiratha the charioteer and his wife Radha, who raised him. The name Radheya. Birth deciding who may compete. Readers hear this moment in different ways. Some hear Draupadi holding the contest to its own terms: her brother announced that birth would count. Some hear her guarding her father's hope for Arjuna. Some hear the old sting of birth used against a man who could clearly do the thing. And some hear all of these at once. The poem doesn't settle it. It moves on. But stay a moment with that glance at the sun. The sun, as we know and the arena doesn't, is Karna's father. He looks up to him in the moment he's turned away, without knowing who he's looking at. Karna and Draupadi will meet again in another hall, later in this serial. For now, the bow is back on the ground, and the arena is waiting for someone else.
screen: `KARNA STRINGS THE BOW.` · `I WILL NOT CHOOSE A SUTA.` · `A LAUGH, AND A GLANCE AT THE SUN.` · `MANY WAYS TO HEAR ONE LINE.`

segments.voice: Breathe, and let the week settle. When the bow went down, Karna looked up at the sun, though he didn't know whose face he was looking for. Bring to mind where you turn when something closes on you: a person, a place, a prayer, a habit, a patch of sky. You don't need to judge it. Just notice it, and notice whether it holds you. Rest there for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Draupadi's swayamvara. Today, Karna at the bow, one sentence from the princess, and a glance at the sun.
Your line: a glance at the sun. Today, when something closes on you, notice where you look first. Day seven hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Karna's story is retold in Hindu storytelling, theater and dance, and in modern novels, some of which tell the whole Mahabharata from his side.

fork.setup: you're Karna. the bow is strung and the arrows ready, and the princess says she won't choose a charioteer's son. what do you do?
fork.reveal: he laughs, a bitter laugh, glances at the sun, and puts the bow down. the text gives him no words at all.

original.note: Sanskrit sūta: a charioteer; the word Draupadi uses for Karna, who was raised by one.

trapdoor: what you thought: Karna failed the test, like the kings before him.
what it means: in Ganguli's version he passes it; one sentence stops him, not the bow.
what a scholar hears: the line turns on the word sūta, the class Karna was raised in, and he answers only with a glance at the sun, his father.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Swayamvara Parva (Karna strings the bow; Draupadi refuses a suta; Karna glances at the sun and puts the bow down)

notes: All paraphrase, including Draupadi's sentence. Confirm in Ganguli that Karna strings the bow, that Draupadi's refusal comes before he shoots, and that he laughs bitterly, glances at the sun and throws the bow aside.

Scholar check: the Pune Critical Edition is reported to omit Karna's attempt and Draupadi's refusal. The script says 'in the version Ganguli translated' and makes no claim about other manuscripts; a Keeper should decide whether to say more.
Week end (days 736–742): the hook looks back over the week. It assumes day 736 is set in the lac house.
The readings of Draupadi's line are unattributed and given without ranking; this is a sensitive moment about birth and caste, and the Keeper should check the framing.
'Karna and Draupadi will meet again in another hall' points ahead to the dice game without telling it.
Editor pass: practice and carry repeated day 733's 'where you're from' exercise; rewritten around Karna's glance at the sun (where you turn when something closes on you).
